KPop Demon Hunters to Götterdämmerung: 11 SSO Concerts to Close 2026
 The DANAMIC Team October 30, 2026 5 minutes read

 Tickets are on sale now for the Singapore Symphony Orchestra (SSO) ‘s final stretch of 2026: eleven programmes running from Sunday, 1 November to Friday, 18 December , all redeemable under the SG Culture Pass . The lineup includes a Halloween organ recital, a family concert that plays “Golden” from KPop Demon Hunters , and a big slab of Wagner. If you’ve been looking for a low-stakes way into classical music, this is the season to try it!
 Back From China, Into Halloween
 The orchestra has come home from what it describes as a well-received seven-city tour of China. It’s heading straight into the spooky stuff with the SSO Organ Series, which gives its Halloween slot to Phantoms and Organs on Sunday, 1 November . Halloween is the night before, and our Halloween parties guide has party season running into the early hours of that Sunday. That makes this recital the calmer way to stretch the weekend out.
 Singaporean organist Phoon Yu plays music by Mendelssohn, Vierne and Bach alongside two of his own compositions, What the Next-Door Neighbour Saw and A Transi for the Common Man . For those, he’s joined by Jeremy Wong on the pipa , a Chinese plucked lute. A homegrown organist premiering pieces with titles that sound like short horror stories is the sort of programming you won’t find in a stuffy concert hall, and it’s the pick for anyone curious but wary.
 Golden, Star Wars and Open Doors
 The concert built for first-timers is SSO Concerts for Children: Family Film Favourites on 14 and 15 November . It covers film scores from Star Wars , Harry Potter , Encanto and more, plus “Golden”, the global hit from KPop Demon Hunters . SSO Associate Conductor Nathanaël Iselin leads the orchestra, with Alasdair Malloy presenting.
 The part that matters most is the format. It’s a relaxed environment performance , which means the usual concert-hall rules are eased so audience members can freely enter and leave the hall when they need to. Classical concerts can feel intimidating because of the quiet, the clapping etiquette and the fear of being stuck in your seat for an hour. This show removes that fear entirely, which makes it ideal for parents with restless kids or an older sibling bringing one along.
 A day earlier, on 13 November , SSO Musical Moments at Woodlands brings a free performance to Woodlands Hospital . SSO musicians perform with singers from the Singapore Symphony Chorus and Youth Choir , which is a lovely move to make a hospital, of all places, one of the season’s stops.
 SSO Musical Moments at Woodlands. Wagner Goes Large on 6 November
 At the opposite end of the scale sits Sibelius and Wagner on 6 November . Finnish conductor Pietari Inkinen opens with Sibelius’s Finlandia and Lemminkäinen’s Return before moving into excerpts from Wagner’s Götterdämmerung , the final opera in his four-part Ring cycle. Soprano Johanna Rusanen joins him, along with the Singapore Symphony Chorus and Youth Choir.
 The SSO calls the Wagner colossal , and that’s a fair word for a piece that ends a cycle about gods, gold and the end of the world. This is the show for anyone who likes their soundtracks loud and their drama unapologetic, so think of it as the original fantasy epic score.
 Then, on 4 and 5 December , Quantedge Music Director Hannu Lintu returns for Hannu Lintu & Steven Isserlis: Schubert and Schumann . The programme pairs Schubert’s “Unfinished” Symphony with Berio’s Rendering , a work inspired by Schubert’s other uncompleted symphony (D. 936A). Cellist Steven Isserlis plays Schumann’s introspective Cello Concerto, and the concert is dedicated to the late Maestro Choo Hoey , the SSO’s founding Music Director.
 A Violin Run Worth Following
 November turns into a violin festival of sorts. Paul Huang plays first in the intimate SSO Chamber Series: Schubert’s Octet with Paul Huang on 19 November . He then plays Dvořák’s Violin Concerto in Lio Kuokman & Paul Huang: Dvořák and Beethoven 7 on 20 and 21 November , where conductor Lio Kuokman adds Unsuk Chin’s subito con forza and Beethoven’s Seventh Symphony.
 On 27 and 28 November , Hannu Lintu conducts Simone Lamsma in John Adams’s Violin Concerto. Copland’s Appalachian Spring and Schumann’s Fourth Symphony complete the bill. Three violin concerts in ten days lets you compare a chamber setting with two full orchestral ones without much planning.
 The one that should be on a young reader’s radar is 2 December . The Singapore National Youth Orchestra (SNYO) , led by Music Director Joshua Tan , plays Brahms’s Third Symphony and Mendelssohn’s The Hebrides . Rising Singaporean violinist Cathy Chen Xi is the soloist in Mendelssohn’s Violin Concerto, and she won first prize in her age category at the Hengqin International Mozart Competition for Young Musicians .
 The SNYO family has more than 180 members aged 10 to 24, drawn from over 70 schools across Singapore. That’s a stage of people who could easily be your classmates or your younger cousins, playing Brahms at full orchestral scale. If you want proof that classical music isn’t only your grandparents’ hobby, this is it. 
 Hannu Lintu and Simone Lamsma. Christmas, Done Two Ways
 The SSO Christmas Concert returns on 11 and 12 December , with the SSO and Singapore Symphony Choruses joining Nathanaël Iselin. Expect traditional Christmas medley singalongs, selections from Tchaikovsky’s The Nutcracker , and John Rutter’s Gloria . The singalong element makes it one of the friendlier entry points on the list.
 The year closes on 17 and 18 December with Singaporean songstress Nathania Ong , joined by vocalists Preston Lim and Vanessa Kee . They’ll perform an evening of musical theatre, Broadway and Disney favourites, conducted by Joshua Tan. It’s a good choice if your playlist leans more Wicked than Wagner.
 Where to Start
 For a first-timer, start with Family Film Favourites . “Golden” and Star Wars are on the programme, and the relaxed rules mean you can step out whenever you need to. For something unusual, Phantoms and Organs brings a local organist, a pipa and two original pieces to the Halloween weekend. For a reason to come back, the SNYO concert on 2 December puts performers your own age front and centre.
 🗓️ Dates: Sunday, 1 November to Friday, 18 December 2026
🎟️ Tickets: On sale now at sso.org.sg
🎭 SG Culture Pass: Tickets are eligible for redemption
🆓 Free Concert: SSO Musical Moments at Woodlands, 13 November, Woodlands Hospital
🚪 Relaxed Environment: Family Film Favourites, 14 and 15 November
🎻 Young Talent: Cathy Chen Xi with the SNYO, 2 December
 Eleven programmes in seven weeks mean there’s something for the KPop fan, the Wagner devotee, and the friend who’s never set foot in a concert hall. Pick one, bring someone who thinks orchestras are boring, and head to the Singapore Symphony Orchestra’s website to book your seats before the year is out!
 Photos and Visuals courtesy of the Singapore Symphony Orchestra, with photography by Otto van den Toorn.
